title: Too many air quality indicators may complicate public messaging for haze: Grace Fu - Yahoo News Singapore
text:

 News Finance More Mail Search the web Advertisement Advertisement Return to homepage Too many air quality indicators may complicate public messaging on haze: Grace Fu
 Chin Hui Shan Updated Tue, 3 November 2026 at 5:23 am UTC 5 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. The NEA currently provides two indicators of air quality: a PSI forecast for the next 24 hours, and an hourly PM2.5 reading. SINGAPORE – Having too many air quality indicators may complicate the Government's messages for the public during haze episodes, said Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu on Nov 3.
 The use of forecast 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) for planning, and hourly PM2.5 for taking decisions, has worked well, she told Parliament.
 "We don't think there is a need to include 12-hour, 24-hour or 48-hour PM2.5 forecasts, as having too many indicators may complicate our public messages," she added.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Fu was responding to a question from the Workers' Party's Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied GRC), who asked if the National Environment Agency (NEA) under her ministry could provide PM2.5 forecasts to help Singaporeans plan their daily activities during the haze.
 "I'm very minded that… our forecast and advisory are clean, succinct, (allowing) people to (easily) manage activities," she said.
 Fu was among five political office-holders who fielded questions on the Government's response to the haze situation – the worst experienced in Singapore in over a decade since the 2015 crisis – over an hour-long debate.
 She had also highlighted how Singapore will, during its ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, work with member states to establish a haze centre and tackle the root causes of the pollution.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development Goh Pei Ming responded to questions on haze safeguards at pre-schools, especially facilities without air-conditioning.
 The impact of the haze on vulnerable workers – including those who work outdoors – and the protections available to them were also addressed by Minister of State for Manpower Dinesh Vasu Dash.
 Overall, Singapore experienced more than seven weeks of haze in 2026. Air quality first entered the unhealthy range on Sept 4, and the Republic was hit with bouts of haze until air quality improved from around Oct 26 .
 The situation also raised questions about the air quality indicators in Singapore, and if they were sufficient in helping people plan their activities.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The NEA provides two indicators of air quality to help people plan their activities: a PSI forecast for the next 24 hours, and an hourly PM2.5 reading.
 PM2.5 are small particles that are the dominant pollutant during transboundary haze episodes.
 The 24-hour PSI forecast indicates what the air quality is expected to be in the next 24 hours and can be used to plan activities ahead of time.
 The forecast takes into account the prevailing air quality, local and regional weather conditions, and the regional hot spot and haze situation assessed through satellite imagery, said Fu.
 Meanwhile, PM2.5 readings refer to concentrations of the dominant pollutant particle during haze episodes. It provides a more reflective indicator of current air quality.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement It is based on the readings from 23 air quality monitoring stations installed across the country.
 People should refer to the PM2.5 values for planning their immediate activities, and to the PSI forecast if they are planning an outdoor activity the next day.
 The NEA will continue to review how its forecasting and public information services can be enhanced to provide more useful guidance, said Fu, adding that providing timely and reliable information is an important part of her ministry's public health response.
 Fu also said that the NEA releases fortnightly forecasts, but noted that these are less accurate as the horizon of the forecasts increases.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The one-hour PM2.5 readings provide the shortest possible forecast and are the "most accurate" in giving the public a sense of the air quality before carrying out an activity, she said.
 On masks, Fu said the priority of the two distribution exercises had been Singaporeans who are more vulnerable to the health effects of haze, or who may have limited means in collecting free haze masks.
 These include seniors, pregnant women, children, individuals with specified medical conditions, holders of CHAS orange and blue cards, those with the Medical Fee Exemption Card, and those on ComCare.
 "This ensures that assistance reaches those who need more support," she said in response to several MPs who had asked about the considerations involved in determining mask eligibility.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement N95 or equivalent masks are generally not required when a person is indoors, or outdoors for short periods, such as when commuting.
 In the case of haze, there is no risk of people-to-people transmission, which would have required all Singaporeans to be masked up as soon as possible, said Fu.
 The criterion for eligibility to collect the masks was expanded in the second round that started on Oct 23, with all Singaporeans aged 60 and above allowed to pick up the face coverings. In the first round, only seniors aged 67 and above were eligible.
 Close to one-third of Singaporeans are eligible under the expanded criterion, she said, adding that close to 30% of them had collected their masks as at Oct 29.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "We will continue to review the scale and eligibility of distribution as conditions evolve, and are prepared to expand support if necessary," she added.
 Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio GRC) also raised questions on whether the ministry has assessed the impact of prolonged haze on agricultural productivity locally and on Singapore's food import sources, and if there are risks to food supply resilience and affordability here.
 Fu said the recent haze has not affected Singapore's food supply.
 "Singapore imports food from more than 180 countries and regions. Sourcing broadly helps to reduce concentration risks and enables industry to switch to alternative sources when needed," she added.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement While wholesalers have given feedback that prolonged haze may impact vegetable growth, Fu said that for local farms, the overall impact has generally been "minimal", with operations returning to normal following the recent improvement in air quality.
 The Singapore Food Agency will continue to monitor the impact on food supply and implement measures to address concerns as necessary, she said.
 Fu also noted that while the haze has affected footfall at hawker centres and markets, this is offset by an increase in takeaway orders.
 She added that NEA will continue to monitor the impact on hawkers, although there is currently no plan to introduce additional haze-specific financial assistance.
